title.value: Analytical Theory of Multicomponent Gas Drives with Two-Phase Mass Transfer

name.value: Stanford University, Department of Petroleum Engineering

note.value: Analytical solutions are constructed by the method of characteristics for dispersion-free flow of multicomponent two-phase mixtures (Helfferich LSSl), with the assumption that the total volume of both phases is invariant with component mixing. An eigenvalue problem is solved to determine the characteristic velocities for a fixed overall composition and composition directions or paths for the displacement process. Previously, the solution route (composition and saturation profiles) to three-component problems was found from these characteristic velocities and composition directions by a systematic elimination of potential eigenvalue paths and shocks. That is, at each step of the solution, an eigenvector was chosen until a path with a single-valued solution was obtained. For displacements with four or more components, however, finding the unique solution route by the systematic elimination technique is very difficult to impossible. In this work, a new technique is used to solve five- and six-component problems for the first time, and is easily extendable to displacements with any number of components. Solutions to nc component problems are shown to be found quite easily by considering additional physical and mathematical conditions that are inherent to nonstrictly hyperbolic conservation laws and phase equilibria. Entropy, velocity, shock and continuity constraints are used to show that solution routes are well posed and confined to lie on nc - 1 key tie lines. Most of these key tie lines (nc-3), called "crossover" tie lines, form a network of tie lines that connect the upstream injection gas tie line with the downstream initial oil tie line. The solution route is shown to move (either by shock or expansion wave) from one crossover tie line to the next across ruled surfaces that are nearly planar. Because the displacement across a ruled surface can be either vaporizing or condensing, the overall solution route can contain nc - 2 vaporizing or condensing gas drive segments. In four-component systems, this is shown to lead to a combined vaporizing and condensing gas drive process.A key result of this thesis is that solutions to gas drive problems are governed by the volatility of the individual components. Components with the highest volatility (large equilibrium K-values) are displaced faster than components with the lowest volatility. The qualitative features of the displacement process for multicomponent oils can be predicted and categorized according to the relative magnitude of the K-values of the injection gas and oil components.The crossover tie lines are also shown to be important in controlling the development of miscibility in gas drive systems. Depending on the magnitude of the K-values of the components in the oil and injection gas, either the crossover, injection gas, or initial oil tie lines controls the development of miscibility. Thus, a new criterion for multicontact miscibility is defined: a displacement is multicontact miscible when any one of the crossover, injection gas or initial oil tie lines becomes a critical tie line. In four-component systems, the crossover tie line is shown to control the development of miscibility in combined condensing/vaporizing gas drive systems. For real field displacements in which most components prefer to be in the liquid phase, the first two or three crossover tie lines will control the development of miscibility.Several analytical solutions for widely varying systems (up to six-component systems) are presented. For example, a two-component alcohol-water system is used to demonstrate the effect of slug size on the displacement process, while three-component systems are used to present the basic mathematical concepts needed to obtain multicomponent solutions. Four-component models are then used to represent more complex multicomponent systems for use in compositional simulations. The effect of varying solvent enrichment on the recovery of hydrocarbons is examined. It is shown that recovery can be very sensitive to modest changes in the enrichment for nearly miscible displacements.
Johns, Russell T. (1992). Analytical Theory of Multicomponent Gas Drives with Two-Phase Mass Transfer. Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: https://purl.stanford.edu/td396km2509
